query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning model that utilizes high-quality experimental and simulation data—including descriptors such as atomic size, mixing enthalpy, density, and thermo-mechanical properties—can rapidly predict refractory HEA compositions that exhibit a superior balance of intrinsic strength, ductility, and low weight compared to compositions designed via conventional thermo-kinetic or simulation methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory HEA compositions developed using conventional iterative experimental processing and thermo-kinetic/simulation approaches.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a data-driven machine learning model trained on existing experimental and simulation datasets to screen the vast compositional space of refractory high-entropy alloys.
generation.conditions: Alloy processing and testing under high-temperature conditions typical for refractory alloys, with the datasets covering a broad range of compositions that are relevant to high-temperature and mechanical load-bearing applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale descriptors such as atomic size, mixing enthalpy, density, and related thermo-mechanical properties that correlate with mechanical performance (strength, ductility, and density).
generation.mechanism: The machine learning model captures nonlinear relationships between the input descriptors and the alloy’s mechanical properties. By learning these correlations, the model identifies compositions that can reconcile the strength–ductility trade-off while reducing density, thus accelerating the alloy design process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy compositions predicted by this model will statistically exhibit a higher strength-to-density ratio and improved ductility relative to baseline alloys derived through conventional methods, within the uncertainty bounds imposed by the available training data.
generation.baseline: RHEA compositions obtained via traditional, time-intensive thermo-kinetic analysis and simulation methods.
generation.boundary: The efficacy of this approach is limited by the quality and representativeness of the training datasets; predictions may be less reliable for compositional regimes that are underrepresented or for which phase stability issues emerge that are not captured in the datasets.
generation.uncertainty: There is inherent uncertainty related to the model’s performance when extrapolating to under-sampled regions of the compositional space and potential unexpected phase instabilities that the existing datasets might not account for.

falsification_experiment.design: Use the machine learning model to predict a set of promising refractory HEA compositions. Synthesize these candidate alloys using established processing techniques and then measure their mechanical properties. Compare the tensile strength, strain-to-failure (ductility), and density of these alloys to those of baseline alloys designed via conventional methods.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the synthesized alloys do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in the strength-to-density ratio and ductility over the baseline alloys, or if the performance improvements fall within the uncertainty bounds of the model predictions, then the hypothesis that a data-driven machine learning approach can rapidly design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight RHEA compositions is falsified.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] . Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . decision.trend: Early studies on refractory high-entropy alloys have focused on detailed experimental processing routes—such as mechanical alloying combined with spark plasma sintering, selective laser melting, and laser powder bed fusion—to optimize phase formation and microstructure for enhanced mechanical properties. These works largely rely on thermo‐kinetic analysis, simulations, and iterative processing trials. While they have successfully demonstrated promising strength and ductility, the approaches are generally time‐ and labor‐intensive and do not provide a rapid, rational framework for traversing the vast compositional space intrinsic to multi‐principal element systems.
decision.unsolved: A rapid and predictive design strategy that can quickly screen the colossal compositional space of refractory HEAs to achieve combinations of intrinsic strength, ductility, and low weight remains elusive.
decision.lever: Develop a machine learning model trained on existing experimental and simulation datasets (e.g., features such as atomic size, mixing enthalpy, density, and thermo-mechanical properties) to rapidly predict optimal alloy compositions that balance strength, ductility, and low weight.
decision.why: Given the trend of extensive but time-consuming experimental and simulation studies, a data-driven approach offers a computational shortcut to screen and optimize the vast design space of multi-principal element refractory alloys. This lever capitalizes on accumulated data to quickly predict promising compositions and thus addresses the core limitation of lacking a quick design method.
